2 *athkhantumuhum*: you overcame them and their wounds multiplied. *Athkhanahu al-jirah*: the wounds weakened him; *al-ithkhan* in everything is its strength and intensity. [Lisan al-Arab, root thkhn].
3 Al-Suyuti said in *al-Durar al-Muntathirah* (p. 342): "It has no basis with this wording." Al-Tirmidhi reported in his *Sunan* (3609), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: They said, "O Messenger of Allah, when were you made a prophet?" He said, "While Adam was between the spirit and the body." Al-Tirmidhi said: "A hasan sahih gharib hadith." And there is a related report from Maysarah al-Fajr.
4 *Al-isr*: a fetter, burden, and confirmed covenant; arduous obligations are called *isr* because they strain and weigh upon the one obligated. His words ﴿and you took upon that My covenant (isri)﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:81] mean My covenant. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/21].
5 Ibn Jarir al-Tabari reported from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib who said: Allah did not send any prophet, from Adam onwards, except that He took from him the covenant concerning Muhammad: if he is sent while [the prophet] is alive, he must believe in him and support him, and he must command his people and take their covenant as well. Then he recited ﴿And [mention] when Allah took the covenant of the prophets...﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:81]. [Mentioned by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 2/253].

Then the Truthful One, glorified is He, says:

﴿That He may question the truthful about their truthfulness. And He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment.﴾ (33:8)

The lam here in ﴿li-yas'ala﴾ (that He may question) is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil). The meaning is: We took the covenant from the prophets, but We will not leave them without being questioned. Why? ﴿That He may question the truthful about their truthfulness.﴾ But if the one who conveys the message is truthful, how is he questioned about his truthfulness?

The questioning of the truthful about their truthfulness is not a rebuke of the truthful; rather, it is a rebuke of those who denied them. God will ask the Messengers: Did you convey this to them? He, exalted is He, says: ﴿On the Day when God will gather the Messengers and say, "What response did you receive?"﴾ (5:109). And God asks the people: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My signs and warning you of the meeting of this your Day?﴾ (6:130).

So the interrogative here is for reproach and rebuke of those who denied.

Or the meaning may be: ﴿That He may question the truthful about their truthfulness﴾ (33:8), i.e., you proclaimed that God is One, so you are truthful, because you took this from Me; and when the Hour arrives and they do not find another god to protect the disbelievers, then You have been truthful in what You reported, and they have been truthful in what they conveyed from Me, since in the Hereafter they found none but the One God.

Therefore He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And he found God with him, and He settled his account in full﴾ (24:39). Had there been with Him another god, he would have defended these disbelievers and prevented them from the punishment.

Likewise, the Messengers are questioned about the resurrection which God promised, which they conveyed to their nations, and about the reckoning and what it contains of reward and punishment. It is as if the Truthful One asks them: Has anything of what I told you failed to come to pass? Did I fall short in rewarding the good-doer or punishing the wrongdoer? Thus: My word is entirely true.

As when you sit with your son, for example, reviewing the study material with him and urging him to study, and he succeeds in the examination; then you ask him: What did you do in answering such-and-such question? You do not intend a true question; rather, you recall together with him the glories of what he has actually accomplished, asking him about God's grant of success to him. Likewise, the Truthful One recalls with the Messengers their standing for the religion of God and their elevation of the word of truth in this Hour, which cannot be turned back.

Thus: the questioning of the truthful about their truthfulness is an honoring of them and a testimony that they discharged what was upon them, and it is likewise a rebuke of those who denied them.(1)

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment﴾ (33:8). The past tense verb here is evidence that everything is prepared and existing in advance, and the Truthful One will not create anything new. Likewise He said of Paradise: ﴿It has been prepared for the God-fearing﴾ (3:133).

We have previously clarified that God, exalted is He, created Paradise to accommodate all people if they believe, and created the Fire likewise to accommodate all people if they disbelieve. That is, there will be no shortage of places. When the people of faith take their places in Paradise, the places of those who disbelieved remain vacant, and God, exalted is He, says to the believers: Take them yourselves:(2) ﴿And that is the Paradise which you have been made to inherit because of what you used to do﴾ (43:72).

The punishment has been described once as painful, once as humiliating, once as great, and once as severe, and each has its own aspect. The painful (alim) points to harshness and causing pain. The humiliating punishment points to the humbling of the one punished and the attack upon his dignity. Some people try to appear stoic, showing endurance of pain and indifference to it, while it hurts them to have their dignity assailed; for such a person the humiliating punishment is fitting.

It is related in illustration of stoicism that a man entered upon Mu'awiya during his illness, while he was showing people that he was well and his health was fine. The man said to him:

"And when death sinks its claws in, you will find every amulet useless."

Mu'awiya perceived his intent and answered him from the same poem of Abu Dhu'ayb:(3)

"And my stoicism before the scorners, to show them
that I do not yield to the calamities of time."(4)

As for the great punishment, its greatness is in its essence, and its magnitude is great—meaning it is not small—or it may be small in body, but its greatness lies in its attributes, or in the persistence of its effect over a long time.

The punishment is described as severe because of the severity of the One who punishes, glorified is He, for when He seizes, He seizes as the Mighty, the Omnipotent.

1. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir at this verse (7/5388):
"It has four aspects:
First: that He may question the prophets about their conveying the message to their peoples; related by al-Naqqash.
Second: that He may question the prophets about the answer their peoples gave them; related by Ali ibn Isa.
Third: that He may question the prophets about fulfilling the covenant He took from them; related by Ibn Shajara.
Fourth: that He may question the truthful tongues about the sincere hearts."
2. On the authority of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is not one of you but he has a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in the Fire. The disbeliever inherits the believer's dwelling in the Fire, and the believer inherits the disbeliever's dwelling in Paradise. That is His saying: ﴿And that is the Paradise which you have been made to inherit because of what you used to do﴾ (43:72)." Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (7/394), attributed to Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh.
3. Attributed by Shihab al-Din Mahmud al-Halabi in his book "Husn al-Tawassul ila Sina'at al-Tarassul," p. 132, to Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali; see Diwan al-Hudhaliyyin, first section, p. 3. [Ibn Manzur also attributed it to Abu Dhu'ayb in Lisan al-Arab, root: d-ʿ-ʿ.]
4. Al-Ḍaʿḍaʿa: humility and abasement. Al-Ḍaʿḍaʿ: the weakest of anything. A man who is ḍaʿḍaʿ is one without opinion or firmness. [Lisan al-Arab, root: ḍ-ʿ-ḍ-ʿ.]

The Exalted says next:

﴿O you who believe, remember the favour of God upon you when armies came against you, and We sent against them a wind and armies you did not see. And God is ever Seeing of what you do.﴾ (33:9)

The Exalted intended to give evidence for His saying to His Messenger in the preceding verses: ﴿And put your trust in God; and sufficient is God as Trustee.﴾ (33:3). So He brought an incident which gathered together all the remnants of his enemies. He had already given him victory over them when they were scattered: first He gave victory over the disbelievers of Makkah at Badr, and over the Jews of Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa'. This time they gathered together to fight him, peace be upon him. Nevertheless, their gathering will not affect the turning away from your call, and you will be given victory over them by armies from God.

So the basis (ḥaythiyyah) of "And put your trust in God" is His saying: ﴿O you who believe, remember the favour of God upon you...﴾ (33:9).

Ni'mah (favour): that which reaches a person with happiness and joy, and whose continuance one seeks. These qualities are found only in faith, because the continuance of the favour in it extends beyond the time of this world to another time which is lasting and enduring in the Hereafter. If the favours of this world are in proportion to your means and capabilities, the favour of the Hereafter is in proportion to the Bestower, the Exalted. So it is, then, the favour of favours.

God Almighty here addresses the believers. The meaning of faith is certainty in the existence of one God who possesses all the attributes of majesty and perfection. God, the Exalted, has made it sufficient for the intellect to be guided to the one creating power which is not opposed. But it is not the work of the intellect to know, for example, the name of this God, nor to know His purpose. Thus, there must necessarily be a communication from God.

We have previously given an example of this: someone knocks on our door. We all agree by intellect that someone is at the door; this is the work of the intellect. But is it the work of the intellect to know who he is, or to know the purpose of his coming? This is what we call conception (taṣawwur).

The bane of the human intellect is that it is not content with rationally grasping a dominant, effective power. It is sufficient for it to understand that behind this universe there is a power, and this power has the attributes of perfection by which it brought this universe into being. But if we want to know what this power is, we must let this visitor tell us about himself, reveal his aim and the reason for his coming. This is achieved only through a messenger who comes from God and tells us about this power, about God, His names and attributes, His method which He has chosen for His creatures, what He has prepared of bliss for those who obey Him, and what He has prepared of punishment for those who disobey Him.

If we deny this messenger and ask for proof of his truthfulness in the communication, he brings forth miracles that confirm him and compel us to believe him, because he came with a kind of thing in which we excel, and a art of our arts, and yet we were unable to produce its like.

So rational thought is the first stage of faith. Therefore, the simplest reply to those who worship other than God is to say to them: What have your gods commanded you? What have they forbidden you? What have they prepared for those who obey them? What have they prepared for those who disobey them? What is the method by which they enslave you?

It is the logic of the intellect that when a messenger from God comes to us, we should turn toward him, face him, and ask him about the riddle of matters of life and the universe that we do not know. It was incumbent upon us to listen to him and submit to his commands, for he came only to deliver us from an intellectual dilemma and a mental predicament that none of us can resolve. The people should have been eager for this Messenger, not opposing and obstinately resisting him, because of the temporal authority they thought would endure.

As for His saying, ﴿remember the favour of God upon you...﴾ (33:9): what is remembrance (dhikr)? When the intellect receives information from the senses, it compares it and sifts it, then retains it in an area of itself that represents a storehouse of information. The intellect in receiving information is like the photographic camera which captures the image in a single exposure, and all people are equal in receiving information; what matters is that the information encounters a mind free of what preoccupies it.

This area of the intellect is called the focus of consciousness (bu'rat al-shu'ur), and it captures only a single mental item. If you wish to recall information from the store, or from the margin of consciousness, it is memory that recalls this information for you and brings it out again from the margin of consciousness into the focus of consciousness.

Then there is what is called the association of meanings (tadā'ī al-ma'ānī), when one thing reminds you of another. There is also imagination (al-mukhayyilah), which fabricates or composes something new from stored information, and we call this imagining (takhayyul). The Arab poet, when he admired the tattoo in green on the skin of a white young woman, imagined it thus:

A maiden whose fingers, in the pattern of the tattoo, in the mail-links of a coat of mail...
A fish of crystal in a net made of chrysolite.

This is an imaginative image specific to the poet; otherwise, which of us has seen a fish of crystal in a net of chrysolite? The poet has his own view of the images he sees. We have previously mentioned the image the poet (Ibn al-Rumi) painted of the hunchback, when he said:

His tendons are shortened and his nape sunk down,
So it is as if he were lying in wait to be slapped.
As if his neck had been slapped once,
So he felt its second and gathered himself.

Since antiquity, poets have regarded the heart as the seat of love and feelings, but this poet comes out to us with another new image from the weaving of his imagination, saying:

The thoughts of your remembrance stir up my affection,
So I feel from them a stirring in the heart.
No limb of mine is without longing in it,
So it is as if my limbs had been created as hearts.

So the meaning of ﴿remember the favour of God upon you...﴾ (33:9) is: do not pass by the favours with heedlessness because of their familiarity to you; rather, remember them always, and place them in the focus of your consciousness. For this reason God made remembrance an act of worship, and it is worship without hardship. When you pray, for example, you spend time and effort on ablution and going to the mosque; likewise when you pay zakat you give from your wealth. But remembrance does not cost you anything.

Therefore, in Surah al-Jumu'ah, when the Exalted calls His servants to prayer, He says: ﴿O you who believe, when the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, then proceed to the remembrance of God and leave off trade...﴾ (62:9). Here there are two movements: a movement of affirmation, by hastening to prayer, and a movement of negation, by leaving off buying and selling and everything that preoccupies you from prayer.

Then He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek of the bounty of God, and remember God often...﴾ (62:10).

In another place He said: ﴿And the remembrance of God is greater.﴾ (29:45). So beware lest you think God wants you to remember Him only at the hour of prayer; rather, I remember Him constantly and always. Although prayer has a time in which it is performed, the remembrance of God has no time. For this reason God made it easy and simple, without hardship, neither in time nor in effort. For in remembering God it suffices that you reflect on the sights upon which your gaze falls, so that you see in them the power of God.

The Exalted reminds us of His favours, because when favours follow one another upon the human soul, the soul becomes accustomed to them, and they become routine, so one does not pay attention to them. For example, you see the sun every morning, yet you rarely remember that it is a sign of the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, and one of His favours, because you have become accustomed to seeing it, and it has become routine for you.

Likewise, the Exalted draws our attention to His favours when He takes them away from others. When you see the sick, you remember the favour of health; when you see the blind, you remember the favour of sight, and so on. At that moment you ought to thank the Bestower who has spared you from what He has afflicted others with. So these exceptional cases God made means of clarification and a reminder to creation of the favours of the Creator.

The word "favour" appears here in the singular, and likewise in His saying: ﴿And if you should count the favour of God, you could not enumerate it.﴾ (14:34). The enemies of Islam among the orientalists stood at this verse and objected that the favour in it is singular, saying: how then can it be counted? This objection of theirs arises from a failure to understand the meanings and stylistic methods of the Qur'an.

We say: what you see as one favour, if you reflected upon it, you would find within it numerous favours exceeding counting. The Qur'an here uses "in" (if), which indicates doubt, because God's favours are not liable to counting and enumeration like the sands of the desert. Has anyone undertaken to count them? For you do not undertake to count something unless it is liable to being counted, and to enumerating what is counted.

Therefore, the Exalted clarifies for us: if you try to enumerate the favours of God, and this will not happen, you will not be able to count them, even though enumeration has become an independent science, with universities and colleges that research and teach it.

You may take one favour of God upon you, then reflect upon it, its elements, its components, its benefits, and its qualities, and you will find within the folds of the single favour various favours. The apple, for example, outwardly is one favour, but in its colours, its taste, the elements of its composition, its smell, and the difference and variety of all this are many favours.

The Exalted made His favours general to the believer and the disbeliever, because He made for them causes, and whoever takes the best of these causes is given, even if he is a disbeliever.

Then we note in His saying, ﴿And if you should count the favour of God, you could not enumerate it﴾ (14:34), that it occurs in the Qur'an twice, and each has a different conclusion. Once He says: ﴿And He gave you of all you asked Him. And if you should count the favour of God, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, mankind is [generally] unjust and ungrateful.﴾ (14:34), and once He says: ﴿And if you should count the favour of God, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (16:18).

In this is an indication that if God treated those upon whom He bestowed favours among creation according to what their faith requires and what their disbelief requires, He would give to the believer and take away from the disbeliever. But He, the Exalted, is Forgiving and Merciful to His creation, and by these two attributes He bestows favours upon all. What you enjoy of God's favours upon you is a trace of forgiveness and mercy: He forgave you your faults first, and ghafr (forgiveness) is to conceal the ugly thing from one who is beneath you.

Then mercy, which is to extend your hand with kindness to one beneath you. We have previously explained that forgiveness precedes mercy, and this is the general rule, but mercy may precede forgiveness, because the removal of the blameworthy thing ought to precede the bestowal of favour, or: the averting of harm takes precedence over the securing of benefit.

We have illustrated this with a thief you find in your house: you first conceal him, not handing him over to the police; then your heart is softened toward him, and you extend your hand to him in kindness. Here forgiveness precedes mercy. But you may deal with him in another way, in which you put mercy before forgiveness. Forgiveness is only from the higher to the lower: you conceal the ugliness of the one who is ugly while you are above him. So one does not say, for example, of a servant, "he concealed it for his master."

Then the Exalted sends us this telegram indicating His support for His believing servants: ﴿when armies came against you, and We sent against them a wind and armies you did not see. And God is ever Seeing of what you do.﴾ (33:9).

The armies herald war, and they are mentioned indefinitely. Then the outcome of this battle comes in these two short clauses: ﴿We sent against them a wind and armies you did not see﴾ (33:9). The nature of these armies is not specified, except that they were from God, who came to repel these disbelievers and nullify their scheming.

(1) al-Khawd: a young maiden of good character, as long as she has not menstruated. It is said: a soft slave-girl. [Lisan al-Arab, root kh-w-d]. Al-mudarrad: the rings of a coat of mail in some of its parts; the meaning is that the tattoo is finely executed, interlaced and intertwined.
(2) al-Zabarjad: emerald; also zabirdaj. [Lisan al-Arab, root z-b-r-j-d].
(3) The poet is Ibn al-Rumi, 'Ali ibn al-'Abbas ibn Jurayj, a great poet of the rank of Bashshar and al-Mutanabbi, of Roman origin; his grandfather was among the clients of the Banu al-'Abbas. Born in Baghdad in 221 AH and raised there, he died there poisoned in 283 AH at the age of 62. [al-A'lam by al-Zirikli 4/297].
(4) al-Akhdi': plural of al-akhda', one of two veins on either side of the neck.
(5) al-Qadhdhal: the joint of the back of the human head. [Lisan al-Arab, root q-dh-l].
(6) That was the day of the Trench in the Battle of the Confederates. Ibn Ishaq said: it was in Shawwal of the fifth year; Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim, on the authority of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the Battle of the Trench was in the fourth year, and the Banu Qurayza were in one day. (Tafsir al-Qurtubi 7/5389).
(7) Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (3/470): "They were the angels; they shook them and cast terror and fear into their hearts, so the chief of each tribe would say: O Banu so-and-so, to me! and they would gather to him, and he would say: Flee! Flee! because of the terror God the Mighty cast into their hearts."

Then he presents an explanatory note clarifying who these troops were:

﴿When they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when the eyes shifted and the hearts reached the throats, and you thought about Allah various thoughts.﴾

This is a description of what took place in the Battle of the Confederates (Ghazwat al-Ahzab), which gathered the remnants of the enemies of the Messenger of Allah. Previously he had fought them when they were scattered, and now they gathered together to fight him, ﷺ. The Quraysh came, and those who followed them from Ghatafan, Asad, Banu Fazara, and others. The Jews came from Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qurayza. It is remarkable that all of these gathered to fight Islam despite the enmity and disagreement that existed among them.

We have said that the People of the Book used to seek victory through the Messenger of Allah over the disbelievers of Makkah, and then the verses came to make the People of the Book witnesses to the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah. The Exalted said: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger." Say, "Sufficient is Allah as a witness between me and you, and [sufficient is] he who has knowledge of the Book."﴾ [Al-Ra'd].

Had the People of the Book considered this testimony, which the Truth, glory be to Him, paired with His own testimony, it would have been incumbent upon them to believe in the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ.

The meaning: ﴿When they came upon you...﴾ [Al-Ahzab] i.e., remember, O Muhammad, and imagine and picture when the confederates came upon you and gathered to fight you. ﴿From above you...﴾ [Al-Ahzab] i.e., from the direction of the east, and they were Ghatafan, Banu Qurayza, and Banu al-Nadir. ﴿And from below you...﴾ [Al-Ahzab] i.e., from the direction of the west, and they were Quraysh and those who followed them from Fazara, Asad, and others. ﴿And when the eyes shifted...﴾ [Al-Ahzab] i.e., remember when the eyes shifted. The meaning of zāgha al-baṣar (the sight swerved) is that it inclined, and from it is the Exalted's saying: ﴿The sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress.﴾ [Al-Najm].

So "zāgha al-abṣār" means they inclined away from their normal direction and their station. Allah created the eye in a particular form, such that it moves upward, downward, to the right, and to the left, and each direction has a name in the language. They say: ra'a, meaning with the corner of the eye; lamaḥa, meaning with the back of the eyelid; and ramaqa, meaning from the side of the nose... etc.

The natural state of the eye is to move in these directions, but when a person is frightened by something, the sight is seized and inclines away from its normal course of turning. Therefore the Exalted says: ﴿Then, behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will be fixed in horror.﴾ [Al-Anbiya'].

And He said: ﴿It only delays them for a Day when eyes will stare in horror.﴾ [Ibrahim]. The staring of the sight (shukhūṣ al-baṣar) is that the upper eyelid rises and the eye fixes on something, not moving to anything else.

In another place the Exalted said about the hypocrites and those who hinder others: ﴿Grudging toward you. And when fear comes, you see them looking at you, their eyes revolving like one who has fainted from death. But when the fear has departed, they will lash you with sharp tongues...﴾ [Al-Ahzab].

Because the terror, at the moment it overtakes the eyes, sometimes fixes the eye on what it sees without it going beyond that out of the intensity of the terror, and sometimes it spins here and there seeking an escape or exit from what it is in. These are states that the frightened and terrified person undergoes.

As for the Exalted's saying: ﴿And the hearts reached the throats...﴾ [Al-Ahzab]: It is well known that the throat (al-hanjara) is the upper part of the windpipe in this known cavity. So how do the hearts reach the throats? This is another effect of terror and fright. When a person is frightened, he is agitated within himself, his heartbeats increase, and his breathing becomes rapid, until from the intensity of the pounding of his heart it seems to him that his heart will be torn from its place. And in colloquial speech they indeed say: "my heart is going to jump out of me" (qalbi hayinut minni).

As for the Exalted's saying: ﴿And you thought about Allah various thoughts.﴾ [Al-Ahzab]

i.e., various conjectures seized them and took hold of them, each having a conjecture that serves his purpose. The believers thought that Allah would not hand them over and would not abandon them, while the disbelievers thought that they would prevail and would uproot the believers so that no one would stand up for them afterward.

We observe in this verse that the Truth, glory be to Him, does not suffice with relating to him what happened, but rather makes him, ﷺ, call the scene to mind himself, saying to him: remember when such-and-such happened.

¹ Ibn Wahb said: I heard Malik say: That was the day of the Trench (al-Khandaq). The Quraysh came from here, the Jews from here, and the Najdis from here. Al-Qurtubi said: Malik means that those who came from above them were Banu Qurayza, and from below them Quraysh and Ghatafan. [Tafsir al-Qurtubi 7/5389].

² Zāgha al-baṣar: it was agitated and did not confirm what it saw. And his saying, describing the fear of some people in Madinah when the enemies surrounded them in the Battle of the Confederates: ﴿And when the eyes shifted (10)﴾ [Al-Ahzab], i.e., they were agitated due to the intensity of the fear. (al-Qamus al-Qawmi 1/294).

(Verse 11) Then the Almighty says:

﴿There the believers were tested, and they were shaken with a severe shaking.﴾

﴿There the believers were tested…﴾ That is: they were tried and examined. So the faith of the strong grew firm, and they said: "Allah will not forsake us." But the hypocrite said: "This is the end of Islam and the Muslims." ﴿…and they were shaken with a severe shaking.﴾ Zilzal (zalzalah, a violent quaking) is a vehement tremor from whose force things become loosened, yet are not uprooted. The meaning is that they were exposed to a severe distress that shook their very foundations, and it distinguished their believers from their hypocrites. Therefore, the Exalted says after it:

{And when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease said, "Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion."} (Verse 12)

Note 1: Hunalika (هنا) is used for what is near in place; hunalika (هنالك) for what is far; and hunaka (هناك) for what is in between. It is also used to indicate time. That is: at that time the believers were tested, so that the sincere might be distinguished from the hypocrite. [Said by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir 7/5406.]

The hypocrites are themselves those in whose hearts there is a sickness; they are one and the same thing, and this kind of conjunction is called ʿaṭf al-bayān (explanatory apposition).

Al-Ghurūr (deception) is that you deceive a person with something that is pleasing in its outward appearance but grieving in its inner reality. You say: "What deceived you about such-and-such a thing?", as if it had something outwardly that deceives you and beguiles you; then when you come to test it, you do not find it to be so.(1)

1 Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, who said: The hypocrites said on the day of the Confederates (al-Aḥzāb), when they saw the confederate armies had surrounded them from every side, and they were in doubt and suspicion regarding the command of Allah, they said: "Muhammad used to promise us the conquest of Persia and Byzantium, and yet we are besieged here to the point that none of us can go out to relieve himself." So Allah revealed: ﴿And when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease said, "Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion."﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 33:12] [Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 6/577].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 33, verse 13:

﴿وَإِذْ.. ( ١٣ )﴾ [al-Ahzab] Here too it carries the sense of: "and remember" (wa-dhkur). ﴿وَإِذْ قَالَت طَّائِفَةٌ مِّنْهُمْ يَا أَهْلَ يَثْرِبَ.. ( ١٣ )﴾ [al-Ahzab] "Yathrib" is the name of the area in which the city (al-Madinah) lies, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) changed its name to "Taybah."

As for the meaning of ﴿لَا مُقَامَ لَكُمْ.. ( ١٣ )﴾ [al-Ahzab], i.e., in the fighting. ﴿فَارْجِعُوا.. ( ١٣ )﴾ [al-Ahzab], meaning: leave Muhammad and his followers on the battlefield and go away. Or ﴿لَا مُقَامَ لَكُمْ ( ١٣ )﴾ [al-Ahzab] means: there is no standing for you upon this religion which you deny in your hearts while lending it support with your outward forms.

Then the Qur'an exposes the stratagem of another group that wants to flee: ﴿وَيَسْتَأْذِنُ فَرِيقٌ مِّنْهُمُ النَّبِيَّ.. ( ١٣ )﴾ [al-Ahzab], i.e., seeking leave not to go out to fight. ﴿يَقُولُونَ إِنَّ بُيُوتَنَا عَوْرَةٌ.. ( ١٣ )﴾ [al-Ahzab], i.e., they are not fortified and do not prevent whoever intends harm against them. It is said: "a house is 'awrah" when it is not secured, or not sturdily built, against whoever approaches it with evil intent, such as when it is low-lying, or its walls are collapsed and easy to climb, or its doors are not secure, etc.

As we say colloquially ("manat"), but Allah the Exalted affirms their lie and nullifies their argument, saying: ﴿وَمَا هِيَ بِعَوْرَةٍ ( ١٣ )﴾ [al-Ahzab], "and they are not exposed." The real cause is ﴿إِن يُرِيدُونَ إِلَّا فِرَارًا ( ١٣ )﴾ [al-Ahzab], i.e., fleeing from the battle, out of fear of its consequences and dread of being killed.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 33, verse 14:

Then He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And if the enemies had entered upon them from all its sides, and then they had been asked to commit disbelief, they would have given it, and they would not have delayed in it except briefly.﴾

﴿Entered upon them﴾ [al-Ahzab] i.e., the houses. ﴿From its sides﴾ [al-Ahzab] from its areas. ﴿Then they were asked to commit disbelief﴾ [al-Ahzab] i.e., they were asked to renounce faith. ﴿They would have given it﴾ [al-Ahzab] meaning: they would have committed disbelief. ﴿And they would not have delayed in it except briefly﴾ [al-Ahzab] meaning: Allah would not have granted them any lingering or residence except briefly, then Allah would take vengeance upon them.(1)

(1) Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir of this verse (3/473): "He, exalted is He, informs about those who ﴿say, Indeed our houses are exposed, while they were not exposed. They intend not but to flee﴾ [al-Ahzab 13]: that if the enemies had entered upon them from every side of the city and from its regions, and then they had been asked to commit fitnah, which is entering into disbelief, they would have disbelieved swiftly, for they do not preserve faith nor hold fast to it even with the slightest fear and alarm. This is how Qatadah, Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd and Ibn Jarir interpreted it."

Meaning of ﴿They had pledged to Allah...﴾ [al-Ahzab 15]: Allah took the covenant from them and they accepted it, and this is what happened at the Pledge of al-Aqabah, when they pledged to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) support and assistance. Or: the statement may refer to a people who missed Badr and missed Uhud, and they said: "By Allah, if we stand in another battle, we will surely show a fine performance in it."

The covenant of Allah is that which you pledge to Allah, and the first covenant you have with Allah, exalted is He, is faith in Him. Since you have believed in Allah, look at what He has asked of you and what He has charged you with, and beware of neglecting any of His commands, because any failure in any obligation from Allah counts as a deficiency in your faith in Allah. It is not fitting for you to break what you have affirmed of faith; rather, it is incumbent upon you to fulfil it, for if you fulfil your part, He will fulfil His part to you as well. So do not take the matter from your side alone, but look to the counterpart.

Know that Allah is watching you; He knows the hidden secrets of hearts and what the breasts conceal. So beware, when you give a pledge, of giving it while intending to break it. Beware of giving a pledge deceptively, for your Lord, glorified and exalted, knows what you do.

1 Yazid ibn Ruman said: They are the Banu Harithah. On the day of Uhud they intended to falter along with the Banu Salamah, but when what was revealed concerning them was revealed, they pledged not to return to the like of it, so Allah reminded them of what they had given of themselves. [Cited by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir 7/5410].

Qur'anic quotations are rendered plainly; the footnote is translated as it stands.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 33, verse 16:

His saying, Exalted is He, to His Prophet ﷺ: (ﷺ) ﴿Say...﴾ (16) [al-Ahzab]. That is, to these people who want to flee from the battle: ﴿Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing﴾ (16) [al-Ahzab]. The Qur'an here is careful regarding the matter of the taking of the soul, and we have already spoken about the difference between death (mawt) and killing (qatl). Therefore, Exalted is He, says about His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Muhammad is nothing but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him. So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾ (144) [Al 'Imran].

Death can be brought about only by the Giver of life, glory be to Him. It occurs first by the releasing of the soul by the command of its Creator, and then the structure is dissolved after it. As for killing, it can be brought about by created beings, and it is completed first by the breaking down of the structure, which entails the taking of the soul, because the structure is no longer fit for the soul to continue in it, after it has lost the qualities required for the soul's remaining.

Flight will not avail in this matter, because it has a specified term, whether it is by God, the Giver of life, or by the act of one of the created beings who disobeys God's command, thus demolishing the structure that God built. And what is the benefit of fleeing from the battle, when we have seen those who witnessed all the battles and then die on their beds? Such as Khalid ibn al-Walid, who said: "I witnessed a hundred charges, or thereabouts, and there is not a handspan of my body without a sword strike or a spear thrust in it, and here I am dying on my bed as a camel dies. May the eyes of the cowards never sleep!" (1)

Then the Qur'an debates with them: suppose you fled from death or killing, would this safety endure for you? Would you live forever in this life? ﴿And then you would not be given enjoyment except for a little﴾ (16) [al-Ahzab]. Life ends swiftly, and you face death, from which there is no escape, and all of us are going to this destination.

1 Mentioned by Ibn Kathir in "al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya" (7/117), and he attributed it to al-Waqidi, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi'l-Zinad, from his father.

Then the Truthful, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Say: "Who is it that can protect you from Allah if He intends harm for you, or intends mercy for you?" And they will not find for themselves, besides Allah, any protector or any helper.﴾ (33:17)

The meaning: Say to them, O Muhammad, "Who is it that ﴿can protect you﴾ [al-Ahzab], that is, can prevent you ﴿from Allah if He intends harm for you, or intends mercy for you﴾ [al-Ahzab], just as He said in another place: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah except for whom He gives mercy﴾ (11:43) [Hud].

So if Allah intends harm for a people, there is no protector for them, because no one can withstand Allah, since there is no other god with Him to ward off harm from these people.

The difficulty that needs clarification here is His saying, ﴿or intends mercy for you﴾ [al-Ahzab]. How can protection (ʿiṣmah) be from mercy? They said: "Here ya'simu (protects) means yamna' (prevents)," and the meaning is: no one can prevent Allah's mercy from you, from your enemies, if Allah intends mercy for you.

We note in the context of the verse that it came in the form of a question, and not in the form of a statement. The Qur'an did not say to Muhammad, ﷺ, "Say, O Muhammad: No one can protect from Allah if He intends you harm," because a declarative sentence may be true or false. Rather, Allah willed to make it an interrogative, performative sentence, so that they themselves would affirm this truth, as if He, exalted is He, were saying to them: "You have accepted your own judgment." And had the Truthful, glory be to Him, not been certain that the answer would only be, "No one," He would not have used this form of question. Thus the interrogative here is more emphatic in establishing the truth of this statement.

Likewise, you resort to this method when replying to someone who denies your favor, saying: "Did I not do good to you on such-and-such a day?" Then he has no recourse but to acknowledge it.

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And they will not find for themselves, besides Allah, any protector or any helper.﴾ (33:17) [al-Ahzab]. The walī (protector, close ally) is the one who is near to you; and you do not draw near to anyone except one whose benefit you hope for. He is the one who is close to you or befriends you; his love precedes the event, and when the event comes, his love for you moves him to defend you.

The naṣīr (helper) is close in meaning to the walī and also defends you, but his defense comes after the event, and he may be one with whom you have no kinship.

The meaning: when Allah wills someone harm, he will not find anyone to prevent him from Allah, neither a walī nor a naṣīr.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 33, verse 18:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Indeed, Allah already knows those who hinder among you and those who say to their brothers, "Come to us," and they do not come to battle except a little.﴾

"Qad" (قد): a particle that conveys certainty, especially when it comes from the Truth, glory be to Him, and the verb that follows it is usually in the past tense. But here, in ﴿قَدْ يَعْلَمُ..﴾ [al-Ahzab], the verb is in the present tense (yaʿlamu). This means that the event taking place now will confirm that Allah knows those who hinder, and He has known it from eternity.

If you say: Allah knows before any hindering takes place, we answer: there is a difference between knowing a matter before it occurs and knowing it as it occurs. A speaker may say, "You knew it beforehand and will repay me for what you knew in advance, but if you leave me in the future, no disobedience will come from me." Therefore the Truth, glory be to Him, wishes to affirm this matter. The "mu'awwiq" (معوِّق, one who hinders) is the one who places obstacles in the way of your aim, weakens your resolve and forsakes you.

His saying ﴿هَلُمَّ إِلَيْنَا..﴾ [al-Ahzab] means: "Come forward and come here." The word "halumma" (هلم, come!) is always used in this singular form, whether addressing one, two, or many, male or female. An example is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿قُلْ هَلُمَّ شُهَدَاءَكُمُ الَّذِينَ يَشْهَدُونَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ حَرَّمَ هَذَا..﴾ [al-An'am: 150], meaning "bring forth." This is the eloquent dialect.

In a dialect of the dialects of Tihama, they attach to it the marks of the dual and plural and of masculine and feminine, saying: halumma, halummi, halumma, halummu, and for feminine plural, halumma(n). (Note: the Arabic forms are "هلم، وهلمي، وهلما، وهلموا، وهلمن".)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿وَلَا يَأْتُونَ الْبَأْسَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا﴾ [al-Ahzab]. "Al-ba's" (البأس) means war, as in His saying: ﴿وَعَلَّمْنَاهُ صَنْعَةَ لَبُوسٍ لَكُمْ لِتُحْصِنَكُمْ مِنْ بَأْسِكُمْ..﴾ [al-Anbiya: 80].

And He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿وَالصَّابِرِينَ فِي الْبَأْسَاء وَالضَّرَّاء وَحِينَ الْبَأْسِ..﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177]. So distinguish between "al-ba's" and "al-ba'sa'": al-ba's is war. As for al-ba'sa', it is everything that befalls a person of harm outside his own self, such as the loss of a child or the loss of wealth, etc. As for al-darra', it is what afflicts a person in his own self, such as illness or the like.

From this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted, about our master Dawud: ﴿وَعَلَّمْنَاهُ صَنْعَةَ لَبُوسٍ لَكُمْ لِتُحْصِنَكُمْ مِنْ بَأْسِكُمْ..﴾ [al-Anbiya: 80].

What is meant is the craft of making armour that a person wears over the places of vital danger in him, and over his vital organs such as the chest, the heart and the head; it has a special covering (al-khawdha, helmet), and the armour is made "musannan" (مسننة), that is, with undulations and hollows, so that it receives the blows of the sword firmly, and the blow does not slip to another place and harm him.

Therefore He, the Exalted, says to His Prophet Dawud about this craft: ﴿وَقَدِّرْ فِي السَّرْدِ..﴾ [Saba': 11], that is, in the precise fitting of these interlocking rings.

Also distinguish here between "libas" (لباس) and "libus" (لبوس): al-libas is what protects a person from the changes of the weather and covers his nakedness during security and the peace of life; these are the ordinary garments that people wear.

In this regard the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿وَاللّهُ جَعَلَ لَكُم مِّمَّا خَلَقَ ظِلاَلاً وَجَعَلَ لَكُم مِّنَ الْجِبَالِ أَكْنَانًا وَجَعَلَ لَكُمْ سَرَابِيلَ تَقِيكُمُ الْحَرَّ وَسَرَابِيلَ تَقِيكُم بَأْسَكُمْ كَذَلِكَ يُتِمُّ نِعْمَتَهُ عَلَيْكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُسْلِمُونَ﴾ [al-Nahl: 81].

As for the word "libus" (لبوس), it is what is prepared for the state of war, such as armour and the like; therefore it came in a form that indicates magnification (libus).

This verse draws our attention to an aspect of the precision of the miraculous Qur'anic expression. The verse mentions "al-harr" (heat) and says nothing of its counterpart, which is cold. Scholars customarily resort to supplying this omitted element when interpreting the verse, saying: "i.e., it protects you from heat and cold," wishing to complete the style of the Qur'an, and this is not permissible.

When we reflect carefully on this verse, we find that Allah, the Exalted, created shade to protect us from the heat of the sun, and made garments, and likewise made for us dwellings in the mountains. Allah created heat in this form which a person cannot bear, because heat has a purpose in our lives: the heat of the sun serves you in many matters, and although it troubles you for some time, the Truth, glory be to Him, kept it to perform a good task for you, then protected you from its evil with shade, clothing and dwellings.

If you say: these things also protect me from cold, we answer: beware of thinking that warmth comes to you from a heavy covering or winter clothes; rather, warmth comes from yourself. You warm the blanket and the bedding on which you sleep, as evidenced by the fact that when you come to your bed to sleep you find it cold, then after the hours of the night pass you find it warm in the morning.

Therefore your own inner heat has passed into the covering and warmed it, and all that the covering does is preserve the heat of your body within it, so that it does not dissipate into the air around you.

Accordingly, when scholars studied the question of the heat of the human body, they found in it a manifestation of the power of Allah: a person radiates heat sufficient, in twenty-four hours, to boil seven litres of water, and the average temperature in the body is a constant 37°, in the scorching heat and the cold of winter, which indicates that your body has an independent nature entirely separate from the atmosphere around you.

Among the wonders of human creation is that this heat varies from one organ to another while the body is one: organs whose temperature is between 7° and 9° (sic) such as the nose, the ear and the eye, and if the temperature of the eye rose above this average it would burst; as for the liver, its temperature is 40°, etc. It is known that heat spreads by conduction within one body and in one place.

Among the wonders of human creation in this matter is the sweat that pours from you when you are exposed to intense heat: the sweat comes out through the pores of the body to lower its temperature and produce a cooling process, like what we see, for example, in a car engine. Even among us farmers, you find that from much work in the land and much sweating a layer like lime forms on the body; these are salts that come out with the sweat. Therefore these farmers eat much "mish" (fermented bread-cheese) and "pickles" to replace the proportion of salts lost with the sweat. Accordingly, the Truth, glory be to Him, did not say "and the cold," because warmth, as we have seen, is intrinsic.

As for His saying: ﴿وَلَا يَأْتُونَ الْبَأْسَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا﴾ [al-Ahzab], this "little" is an exception: either from the act of coming, or they do come to war, but a few of them fight with resolve and energy, while the rest came only as "dhar al-ramad fi al-'uyun" (throwing ash in the eyes), as they say, and so that they would not be accused of lagging behind the Messenger of Allah.

1 Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning His saying: ﴿قَدْ يَعْلَمُ اللَّهُ الْمُعَوِّقِينَ مِنكُمْ..﴾ [al-Ahzab: 18], he said: This was on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab). A man left the presence of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and found his brother before him with roasted meat and a loaf of bread. He said to him: "You are here with the roast meat, the bread and the date wine, while the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is among the spears and swords." He said: "Come to me, for you and your companion have gone too far." (He swore by Him in whose name he swears: "Muhammad will never be given water for them." He said: "You lie"), by Him in whose name he swears, and he was his brother from the same father and mother. "By Allah, I will inform the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, of your affair." He went to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to inform him, and found that Jibril, peace be upon him, had already descended with the news: ﴿قَدْ يَعْلَمُ اللَّهُ الْمُعَوِّقِينَ مِنكُمْ وَالْقَائِلِينَ لِإِخْوَانِهِمْ هَلُمَّ إِلَيْنَا وَلَا يَأْتُونَ الْبَأْسَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا﴾ [al-Ahzab]. [Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 6/580].

Then the Exalted says:

﴿Stingy towards you. And when fear comes, you see them looking at you, their eyes rolling like one who faints from the approach of death. But when fear departs, they lash at you with sharp tongues, stingy with regard to good. Those have not believed, so Allah has nullified their deeds, and that is ever easy for Allah.﴾ (33:19)

The utterance of the Exalted, ﴿Stingy towards you…﴾ (33:19) [al-Ahzab]. Shuh (stinginess) in its general meaning is miserliness, but the shahih (stingy person) is one who is stingy towards others, and may be generous towards himself and his family, whereas the bakhil (miserly person) is one who is stingy even towards himself. Therefore the Exalted said ﴿Stingy towards you…﴾ (33:19) [al-Ahzab], not towards themselves.(1)

When you reflect upon the blameworthy traits in the universe, you find them necessary for the realities of the universe's creation, and you find a task for them. Therefore the poet became aware of this matter, and said:

The stingy are the most generous of people, all of them,
For they possessed the world and did not benefit from it.
They did not deprive people of some of what they possessed,
Except that they might give away all that they had gathered.

Another, seeing a favour of the miser over him, says:

"The miser's favour upon me, I repay with a good deed, for it lightens me in my own soul."

Indeed, the miser is light upon the soul, because he has not done you any favour by which he could enslave you, nor has he ever enslaved you on any day by kindness towards you; so he is light upon your soul, because you are not indebted to him for anything.

This is in accordance with the saying of the poet:

Do good to people and you will enslave their hearts,
And man has often been enslaved by kindness.

Thus stinginess, though blameworthy, has been placed by God in some natures in order to make opposites complement each other. The meaning of "complementing opposites" is that stinginess has as its counterpart generosity, and the miser assists the generous in performing his task. The generous person is customarily (loose-handed), spending here and there until what he has runs out; and among the people of generosity are those who resort to selling their land or house for the sake of their generosity. So who would buy from him, if there were no one who hoards money and withholds it?

Therefore: if you look at everything in existence, you will find for it a task, even if it is blameworthy. Moreover, the miser is often a witty person whose gathering is never free of his wit. In the early days of our youth we used to smoke cigarettes; one of us would take out a pack of cigarettes and distribute them to those present, and perhaps one would not suffice, so I would take out another. In our gathering there was one of these people, and he looked at me in anger and said: "[May] your heart [be cut], my brother!"

And these cigarettes were a cause of our ruin in our youth, and this had a profound effect on us in old age. So let the youth guard their youth, and not destroy it with such forbidden filth.

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿…and when fear comes, you see them looking at you, their eyes rolling…﴾ (33:19) [al-Ahzab]. That is, at the moment of terror, fear seizes their sight, so they look here and there; their gaze does not settle and does not rest upon anything; their eyes are dazed. ﴿…like one who faints from the approach of death…﴾ (33:19) [al-Ahzab].

From this is the report: "You are numerous at the time of fear, and few at the time of greed."

This was their state at the time of fear and terror. ﴿But when fear departs, they lash at you with sharp tongues…﴾ (33:19) [al-Ahzab]. The meaning of ﴿they lash at you…﴾ (33:19) [al-Ahzab] is that they hurt and harm you with their tongues, saying to you: "Give us our share, for we fought alongside you, and had it not been for us you would not have prevailed over your enemy," and other forms of verbal abuse, injury and reproach.

All of this is among the meanings of (salq), from which comes: salaq the meat or the like, which means to boil it in water without adding anything to it; and similar to it is salkh (skinning), for all these meanings converge in causing pain.

In language, you commonly find that when two words share two letters and differ in the third, they have a general meaning that unites them, as in salaq and salakh, and in qataf, qatar, and qatam; all of them converge in separation.

The utterance of the Exalted, ﴿…with sharp tongues…﴾ (33:19) [al-Ahzab]: "ḥidād" means sharp, eloquent, full-mouthed, as in His saying: ﴿So your sight today is sharp﴾ (50:22) [Qaf].

The meaning of ﴿…stingy with regard to good…﴾ (33:19) [al-Ahzab], after He had said ﴿…stingy towards you…﴾ (33:19) [al-Ahzab], is that He emphasised this meaning by saying ﴿…stingy with regard to good…﴾ (33:19) [al-Ahzab], that is, in its entirety.

﴿Those have not believed…﴾ (33:19) [al-Ahzab], for had they believed, they would have known that stinginess is a stinginess against themselves, not in their interest, because the generous person seeks increase of giving from God, whereas the stingy person has no increase. Therefore the Exalted says: ﴿Here you are, being called to spend in the way of Allah, but among you are those who withhold; and whoever withholds, withholds only from himself…﴾ (47:38) [Muhammad].

And your Lord, when He sees you spending from what He has given you, increases it for you, because you are entrusted with provision. Therefore one of the righteous says: "O Allah, You have accustomed me to goodness, and You have accustomed Your creatures to goodness; so do not cut off what You have accustomed me to, lest I cut off from people what I have accustomed them to." So giving is a means of drawing forth the favour of Allah and a cause of more of it.

Suppose you have several children, and you give one of them a pound, for example; he goes and buys sweets with it, then distributes them among his siblings and does not prefer himself over them. Undoubtedly you will entrust him and give him more, because goodness in his hand overflows to others.

And the consequence of not believing is ﴿So Allah has nullified their deeds, and that is ever easy for Allah﴾ (33:19) [al-Ahzab]. That is, they performed deeds, but their deeds have no capital of faith, therefore Allah nullified them, that is, made them without benefit or gain returning to them. This matter the Qur'an clarified in His saying: ﴿The example of those who disbelieve in their Lord is that their deeds are like ashes which the wind blows hard on a stormy day; they have no power over anything of what they earned. That is the far-reaching error﴾ (14:18) [Ibrahim].

This nullification is an easy matter for Allah, the Exalted. But in regard to the right of Allah, do we say: this is difficult, and this is easy? They say: every command of Allah is easy, because He, the Exalted, does not act by processing a thing; rather He acts, glory be to Him, by "Be" (kun). We have previously given an example of processing actions: one who wishes to move, for instance, ten ardabs of wheat, cannot but carry them in portions, so he moves a sack (jawal) from here to there, then another, until he finishes the whole quantity, and he takes time for this work in proportion to his strength.

When knowledge advanced and human thought developed, we saw a machine that carries this whole quantity and moves it in a single motion, merely by pressing a set of buttons and switches. If the servant created by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has been able to attain this facilitation, then what of the Creator, the Mighty and Majestic?

Therefore He, the Exalted, says: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ (36:82) [Ya-Sin]. Do not be surprised at this matter, for your Lord has given you in your own self a share of it. Why do you marvel at the act of Allah the Exalted by "Be," when you see your limbs respond merely to your willing the act — the mere desire to stand, and you find yourself standing, without even commanding your limbs and muscles to stand?

If you say: why then does a person not command his limbs and organs as he wishes? We say: because you cannot command them; rather they obey you and your will by the command of Allah. All things are indeed under the command of the Creator, the Exalted, and never deviate from His command. Have you not read about the heaven: ﴿and it has listened to its Lord and was obligated﴾ (84:2) [al-Inshiqaq].

So the heaven, despite its great creation, listens and obeys the command of its Creator. But you, O servant, what do you command, when you do not even know what you are commanding? Do you know the muscles, organs and nerves that participate within you to perform the act of standing? Therefore, because you do not know what you command, Allah made your organs and limbs respond merely to your will.

As for Him, the Exalted, He says "Be," because He is the Creator of everything, and everything is under His command. And He, the Exalted, said "Be" so that you need not say it yourself; it is as though it had preceded from Him, the Exalted, for your benefit, and you act from the inner depth of that first "Be," which has been distributed among us all.

(1) Al-Qurtubi, in his tafsir (12/7-8 [edition reference 7541]), cites several opinions on the interpretation of His saying ﴿stingy towards you…﴾ (33:19) [al-Ahzab]:
– "Stingy towards you": that is, with regard to digging the trench and spending in the way of Allah. Said by Mujahid and Qatadah.
– It was said: with regard to fighting alongside you.
– It was said: with regard to spending on your poor and needy.
– It was said: stingy with the spoils when they obtain them. Said by al-Suddi.

The Noble Qur'an recounts this situation concerning the hypocrites and exposes their evil intentions. After the confederates (al-Ahzab) gathered and set out to fight the Prophet (ﷺ), these hypocrites still ﴿think the confederates have not gone away﴾ [al-Ahzab]. This gathering frightens and terrifies them, so they did not believe in it. They had seen the Prophet (ﷺ) defeat his enemies when they were scattered, and this was the first time the enemies of Islam had gathered together despite their differences.

So the hypocrites found it hard to believe that the confederates had assembled in this way, and after that they dispersed without producing any event worth recording in history.

Al-husban (الحسبان): it means ظن (zann, supposition), that is, it is not a reality.

﴿And if the confederates should come, they would wish that they were out in the desert among the Bedouins﴾ [al-Ahzab]. That is: if the confederates were to gather, the hypocrites would wish that they were ﴿out in the desert among the Bedouins﴾, meaning living in the open country far from Madinah, because they fear any kind of gathering, and because if they stayed in Madinah they would either have to fight the confederates while doubting victory, or refrain from fighting and thereby become enemies of the Muslims.

They therefore want to remain in hypocrisy and not to leave it, and so they wish for the life of the desert with the Bedouins. And from afar they ﴿ask about your news﴾ [al-Ahzab], meaning: what happened to you in this confrontation.

Then the Qur'an establishes this reality: ﴿And had they been among you, they would not have fought except a little﴾ [al-Ahzab]. That is, to ward off suspicion and to throw dust in people's eyes. So do not grieve over them, and do not be saddened by their staying behind.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 33, verse 21:

Uswa (ʾuswah): a model and a behavioural example. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ conveys from Allah His method for safeguarding human conduct in life, and he is also ﷺ a model of behaviour. How easy it is for a person to admonish and to speak; what matters is that he acts in accordance with the content of his words and his intent. Thus was our master, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, both a conveyer and a model of conduct. For this reason, his wife Lady ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said of him: "His character was the Qur'an."

But what is the good model that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ presented in the matter of the Confederates (al-Aḥzab)? When the confederates gathered, one of his ﷺ supplications was: "O Allah, Revealer of the Book, swift in reckoning, defeat the confederates. O Allah, defeat them and shake them." (1)

Later he ﷺ made his creedal motto: "There is no god but Allah alone; He fulfilled His promise, granted victory to His servant, honoured His soldiers, and defeated the confederates alone." (2) Since this is the motto of the Chosen One ﷺ, it is a good model for you.

Allah the Exalted said about the believers in this battle: ﴿And they were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of Allah?"﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 214].

At Badr, Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of Allah, some of your pleading with your Lord is enough; Allah will surely fulfil for you what He has promised you."

Someone may say: If Allah the Exalted had promised His Prophet victory, why the insistence in supplication? We say: Our master, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, did not insist in supplication for victory, because it was a certain promise from Allah the Exalted.

Read His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And [recall] when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours, and you wished that the unarmed one would be yours. But Allah wanted to establish the truth by His words and cut off the last of the disbelievers﴾ [Al-Anfal: 7].

So the Messenger did not desire victory over the caravan, nor over the trade of Quraysh; rather he desired the armed force that had come out for war.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿In the Messenger of Allah there is for you an excellent example﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 21]. It is as if the good model has its place in the whole of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: he ﷺ is a vessel for the good model in every limb of his ﷺ. In his tongue there is a good model, in his eye a good model, in his hand a good model... etc. All of him ﷺ is a good model.

For whom is this model? ﴿For whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day and remembers Allah often﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 21].

The remembrance of Allah is described as being frequent, because the obligations of faith require the soul to prepare and get ready for them, and they lead to hardship. As for the remembrance of Allah, as we have said, it does not burden you with anything and does not weigh on you. Therefore the Exalted said: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾ [Al-ʿAnkabut: 45].

That is: greater than any other act of obedience, because it is easy upon your tongue; you can perform it in every action of yours, at every time, and in every place. For this reason we said concerning the verse of Friday: ﴿And when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land and seek from the bounty of Allah, and remember Allah often﴾ [Al-Jumu'ah: 10].

(1) A hadith agreed upon (Muttafaq ʿalayh), narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (2933), and likewise Muslim in his Sahih (1742), Kitab al-Jihad, Bab Istihbab al-Du'a bil-Nasr (7), from the hadith of ʿAbdullah ibn Abi Awfa.

(2) A hadith agreed upon, narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (4114), and likewise Muslim in his Sahih (2724), Kitab al-Dhikr wal-Du'a, Bab (18), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, and their wording is: "There is no god but Allah alone; He honoured His soldiers, granted victory to His servant, and defeated the confederates alone, with nothing after Him."

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 33, verse 22:

Meaning: When the believers saw the confederates retreating in defeat, ﴿They said, "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us, and Allah and His Messenger have spoken truly." And it increased them only in faith and submission.﴾ [Al-Ahzab 33:22] That is, this victory and this promise that has come to pass ﴿increased them only in faith and submission.﴾

This matter is one of the proofs that faith (iman) increases and decreases. Faith increases with the increase of the particulars that complete it. After faith in the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, there is faith in the particulars that confirm the truth of the Truth in every event.

"Submission" (taslim): that is, submission to Allah in everything He brings about for His servants.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 33, verse 23:

This verse was revealed concerning a group of believers whose faith was sincere(1), except that they had not witnessed Badr or Uhud. Yet they had pledged to God that if another battle came, they would hasten to it and display excellent valor in it.

It is also reported that it was revealed concerning Anas ibn al-Nadr. When he missed Badr, he pledged to God that if another battle with the polytheists came, he would display excellent valor in it. And indeed, when Uhud came, he displayed excellent valor in it until he was martyred there. They found in his body more than eighty wounds from spear thrusts and sword blows(2). This is the meaning of ﴿They have been true to that which they promised Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab].

Whenever you hear the word ﴿men﴾ [al-Ahzab] in the Qur'an, know that the context is one of earnestness and steadfastness upon the truth, and of pride in firm resolves that do not bend, and hearts in which faith has taken root like mountains. These men fulfilled the covenant they had made before God with respect to themselves, that they would display valor in the cause of supporting Islam, even if the matter came to martyrdom.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Among them is he who has fulfilled his vow, and among them is he who awaits﴾ [al-Ahzab]: "fulfilled his vow" means he completed what he had vowed, i.e., he died. The word "nahb" originally means a vow, so the intended meaning is that he discharged what he had vowed, or what he had covenanted with God regarding fighting. Then "al-nahb" was used with the meaning of death.

But what is the connection between a vow and death? They said: the meaning is that when you make a vow, make your life the price for fulfilling this vow. This expression ﴿Among them is he who has fulfilled his vow﴾ [al-Ahzab] comes so that you know that death must be a vow from you. That is: vow to God that you will die, but in supporting the truth and in the cause of God. Thus the believer is one who vows himself and his soul to God, and death in his view is something sought so that it may be in the cause of God.

When the believer keeps the matter of death in mind and reflects upon it, he sees that all creation has died from the time of Adam, peace be upon him, until now. Therefore his life becomes light to him so long as it is in the cause of God, so he vows it and offers it to God willingly. And why not, since he has sacrificed a life whose destiny is to perish, and has purchased in exchange a lasting and eternal life of bliss.

It has been reported in a narration: "I have never seen a certainty more like doubt than people's certainty about death." Although we see that death does not spare any of us, yet each person imagines in himself that he will not die.

It is right for the believer to vow himself and to sacrifice himself in the cause of God, because God says: ﴿And never think of those who have been killed in the cause of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for. They rejoice in what Allah has bestowed upon them of His bounty and rejoice for those who have not yet joined them from behind them—that there is no fear concerning them, nor do they grieve. They rejoice in a favor from Allah and bounty and that Allah does not allow to be lost the reward of the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran].

And this life which is with God is life in reality, because provision is the mark of the living one who lives, eats, and drinks, etc. Beware lest you think it is merely a spiritual life.

You may hear someone say: "Does this mean that if I opened the grave of one of the martyrs, I would find him alive in his grave?" We say to whoever wishes to dispute this matter: God, exalted is He, said ﴿alive with their Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran] and did not say "alive with you." So do not judge this life by your own law; do not transfer the law of this world to the law of the Hereafter.

The believer ought to hold his belief about death as some of the knowers ('arifin) said: "Death is an arrow that has been shot at you in actuality, and your life is according to the distance of its journey toward you."

When the Qur'an treats this matter, He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion, and He is over all things competent. He who created death and life...﴾ [al-Mulk]. So He mentioned death before life, so that we do not receive life with the delusion of life, but receive it together with its opposite, so that we are not deceived by it.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And among them is he who awaits﴾ [al-Ahzab]: that is, he awaits the fulfillment of his covenant with God. It is as if God, exalted is He, says: the good in you, O community of Muhammad, remains until the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And they did not change at all﴾ [al-Ahzab]. The meaning of "tabdil" (change) here: they did not falter in anything they had covenanted with God and vowed, so no battle came afterward in which any of them held back, nor did any of them enter the battle with duplicity and show-off, fighting from afar or retreating out of fear of death; rather they were in the thick of it until martyrdom.

(1) ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib said concerning Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbaydillāh: "That is a man concerning whom a verse of the Book of God was revealed: ﴿Among them is he who has fulfilled his vow, and among them is he who awaits﴾ [al-Ahzab]. Ṭalḥa is among those who have fulfilled their vow; there is no reckoning against him for what is to come." And ʿĪsā ibn Ṭalḥa said: The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, passed by Ṭalḥa and said: "This is among those who have fulfilled their vow." Both are cited by al-Wahidi al-Nisaburi in (Asbab al-Nuzul, pp. 202–203).

(2) From Anas ibn Malik, who said: My uncle Anas ibn al-Nadr was absent from the battle of Badr, and it grieved him. He said: "I missed the first scene that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, witnessed. By God, if God, glorified is He, lets me witness a battle, God will see what I do." When the day of Uhud came and the Muslims were routed, he said: "O God, I disavow before You what these polytheists have brought, and I apologize to You for what these have done"—meaning the Muslims. Then he walked forward with his sword, and Saʿd ibn Muʿādh met him, and he said: "O Saʿd, by Him in whose hand my soul is, I find the scent of Paradise beyond Uhud." He fought them until he was killed. Anas said: We found him among the slain with more than eighty wounds, among them a sword blow, a spear thrust, and an arrow shot, and they had mutilated him, and we did not recognize him until his sister recognized him by his fingertips. And this verse was revealed. [Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi, p. 202; and Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kabir (4/329)].

Then the Truthful One, glory be to Him, says:

﴿That Allah may reward the truthful for their truthfulness, and punish the hypocrites if He wills, or turn to them in forgiveness. Indeed Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ (33:24)

Reflect here on the mercy of the Creator toward creation, a mercy from which not even the hypocrite has been deprived. He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿and punish the hypocrites if He wills, or turn to them in forgiveness..﴾ (33:24).

We have already spoken about the two attributes of forgiveness and mercy, and we said: "Ghafur Rahim" (Forgiving, Merciful) are forms of intensification (ṣīghat al-mubālagha), indicating the abundance of forgiveness and the abundance of mercy. The Qur'an often pairs them, for forgiveness comes first to cover over the flaw and the deficiencies, and then mercy follows it from Allah, in that His hand extends with kindness.

We clarified this with the example of a thief you find in your house: you pity him, then your hand reaches out to him with help that enables him to avoid repeating such an act. We also said that, generally, forgiveness precedes mercy, and rarely does mercy precede forgiveness.

And we said that forgiveness is conditioned on being from the higher to the lower: if a servant covers over an ugly deed of his master, it is not said that he "forgave" him. Likewise with mercy: if the lesser extends kindness to the higher, it is not called mercy, because he may be giving it in return for what was done for him, or giving it in expectation that the like of what he gave will be returned to him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 33, verse 25:

Then the Truthful Lord says:

﴿And Allah turned back those who disbelieved, in their rage, not having obtained any good. And Allah sufficed the believers in the fighting. And Allah is ever Powerful and Mighty.﴾ (33:25)

Al-ghayz (rage): the seething of the heart's resentment against a rival opponent. The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, turned back the disbelievers while rage filled their hearts, because they came and went away without gaining anything from the Muslims. ﴿Not having obtained any good⦆ (33:25) does not mean absolute good; rather, they did not obtain good in their own estimation, namely the victory over the Muslims that they sought. For them, that would have been good, even if it was evil intended for Islam.

Allah turned back the disbelievers without any return, and they will not think again of attacking Islam after that. Therefore, when they departed frustrated, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "They will never attack us again; rather, we will attack them." (1) And indeed, after that came the conquest of Makkah.

As for His saying, ﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in the fighting⦆ (33:25), meaning: the turning back of the disbelievers was not due to your strength and fighting; rather, Allah undertook their repulse and spared you the fighting. True, there were skirmishes that did not reach the scale of a battle, and had a battle actually taken place, it would have been to the disadvantage of the believers, for they were three thousand while the polytheists were ten thousand.

Thus, Allah's mercy toward the believers was the principal cause of the victory. Therefore the verse was concluded with His saying: ﴿And Allah is ever Powerful and Mighty⦆ (33:25): Powerful, who grants you victory without fighting on your part; and Mighty, meaning He overcomes and is not overcome.

This is the matter concerning Quraysh and its allies. As for the Banu Qurayzah, Allah says concerning them:

﴿And He brought down those who supported them among the People of the Scripture from their fortresses and cast terror into their hearts. A party you killed, and a party you took captive.⦆ (33:26)

(1) Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (4109, 4110), and Ahmad in his Musnad (4/262), from the hadith of Sulayman ibn Surad. Al-'Asqalani said in Fath al-Bari (7/405): "In it is one of the signs of prophethood, for the Prophet (ﷺ) performed 'umrah in the year of the truce, and Quraysh prevented him from the House, and a truce was made between them until they broke it, and that was the cause of the conquest of Makkah, so the matter happened as he had said."

Meaning of ﴿ظَاهَرُوهُم﴾ [Al-Ahzab]: that is, they aided them. ﴿مِن صَيَاصِيهِمْ﴾ [Al-Ahzab]: that is, from their fortresses and strongholds. ﴿وَقَذَفَ فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ الرُّعْبَ﴾ [Al-Ahzab]: that is, fear, and it is one of the soldiers of Allah. This terror which Allah cast into the hearts of the disbelievers is what scattered them, and He did not give the great number they had any value. And what use are large numbers that are frightened and panicked? ﴿يَحْسَبُونَ كُلَّ صَيْحَةٍ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ [Al-Munafiqun].

Did not the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) tell us that they used the siwak (tooth-stick), so the disbelievers thought they were sharpening their teeth to devour them? This is the terror with which Allah granted victory to His believing servants. The meaning of ﴿فَرِيقًا تَقْتُلُونَ﴾ [Al-Ahzab]: that is, the fighters who bear arms. ﴿وَتَأْسِرُونَ فَرِيقًا﴾ [Al-Ahzab]: and they are the women, the children, and others who do not bear arms.

﴿And He caused you to inherit their land, their homes, and their wealth, and a land you had not trodden. And Allah is ever Competent over all things.﴾ (27)

The meaning of ﴿And He caused you to inherit...﴾ (27) [al-Ahzab]: that is, He gave you the land, homes, and wealth of your enemies after their decline and defeat. ﴿And a land you had not trodden...﴾ (27) [al-Ahzab]: that is, new places you had not yet gone to. The intended meaning is Khaybar. It is as if Allah were saying to them: wait, for you will take much from them. ﴿And Allah is ever Competent over all things.﴾ (27) [al-Ahzab].

Thus ends the Qur'anic account of the Confederates (al-Ahzab).

Now we should review the story through the philosophy of its events, and speak of the heroism it contains. It contains many heroic acts, and each hero has a role.

The story begins when Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Sallam ibn Abi al-Huqayq, both from Banu Qurayza, went to the Quraysh in their places and said: "We have come to you to cooperate with you in nullifying the call of Muhammad. You come from below, and we will descend from above, and we will surround Muhammad and those with him and finish them off."

Among the Quraysh there was some sense, so they said to Huyayy ibn Akhtab and his companion: "You are People of the Book and more knowledgeable about religious matters. Tell us: is our religion, which we follow, better, or the religion of Muhammad?" He said: "Rather, you are the people of truth."

The Quraysh heard these words with their own desires, and as it is said: the calamity of opinion is desire. Therefore they did not debate this matter with him; rather, they wove upon his pattern. They did not mention what the People of the Book had done before his mission (ﷺ), that they used to seek victory over the disbelievers through the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying to them: "The time of a new prophet has drawn near, whom we will follow, and with him we will kill you as 'Ad and Iram were killed." The Quraysh failed to consult Huyayy ibn Akhtab and to ask him: why did you change your opinion about Muhammad?

Then the Qur'an came afterward and exposed both these and those. He, glorified be He, said: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They believe in jibt and taghut, and they say to those who disbelieve, "These are better guided than those who believe in the way."﴾ (51) [al-Nisa'].
